title: Definition of a hydrocarbon
statement: define the term hydrocarbon as a compound made up of $\ce{C}$ and $\ce{H}$ atoms only

title: Alkanes as hydrocarbons without functional groups
statement: understand that alkanes are simple hydrocarbons with no functional group

title: Functional groups determine properties
statement: understand that the compounds in the table on pages 29 and 30 contain a functional group which dictates their physical and chemical properties

title: General, structural, displayed and skeletal formulas
statement: interpret and use the general, structural, displayed and skeletal formulas of the classes of compound stated in the table on pages 29 and 30

title: IUPAC nomenclature of organic molecules
statement: understand and use systematic nomenclature of simple aliphatic organic molecules with functional groups detailed in the table on pages 29 and 30, up to six carbon atoms (six plus six for esters, straight chains only for esters and nitriles)

title: Deducing molecular and empirical formula
statement: deduce the molecular and/or empirical formula of a compound, given its structural, displayed or skeletal formula

title: Key organic chemistry terminology
statement: interpret and use the following terminology associated with types of organic compounds and reactions: (a) homologous series (b) saturated and unsaturated (c) homolytic and heterolytic fission (d) free radical, initiation, propagation, termination (e) nucleophile, electrophile, nucleophilic, electrophilic (f) addition, substitution, elimination, hydrolysis, condensation (g) oxidation and reduction (in equations for organic redox reactions, the symbol [O] can be used to represent one atom of oxygen from an oxidising agent and the symbol [H] to represent one atom of hydrogen from a reducing agent)

title: Types of organic reaction mechanisms
statement: understand and use the following terminology associated with types of organic mechanisms: (a) free-radical substitution (b) electrophilic addition (c) nucleophilic substitution (d) nucleophilic addition (in organic reaction mechanisms, the use of curly arrows to represent movement of electron pairs is expected; the arrow should begin at a bond or a lone pair of electrons)

title: Straight-chain, branched and cyclic molecules
statement: describe organic molecules as either straight-chained, branched or cyclic

title: Shapes from sp, sp2 and sp3 hybridisation
statement: describe and explain the shape of, and bond angles in, molecules containing $sp$, $sp^2$ and $sp^3$ hybridised atoms

title: Sigma and pi bonds in hybridised atoms
statement: describe the arrangement of σ and π bonds in molecules containing $sp$, $sp^2$ and $sp^3$ hybridised atoms

title: Planar arrangement in organic molecules
statement: understand and use the term planar when describing the arrangement of atoms in organic molecules, for example ethene

title: Types of structural isomerism
statement: describe structural isomerism and its division into chain, positional and functional group isomerism

title: Types of stereoisomerism
statement: describe stereoisomerism and its division into geometrical (cis/trans) and optical isomerism (use of E/Z nomenclature is acceptable but is not required)

title: Cis-trans isomerism in alkenes
statement: describe geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism in alkenes, and explain its origin in terms of restricted rotation due to the presence of π bonds

title: Chiral centres and enantiomers
statement: explain what is meant by a chiral centre and that such a centre gives rise to two optical isomers (enantiomers) (Candidates should appreciate that compounds can contain more than one chiral centre, but knowledge of meso compounds, or nomenclature such as diastereoisomers is not required.)

title: Identifying chiral and geometrical isomerism
statement: identify chiral centres and geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism in a molecule of given structural formula including cyclic compounds

title: Deducing isomers from molecular formula
statement: deduce the possible isomers for an organic molecule of known molecular formula

title: Preparing alkanes: hydrogenation and cracking
statement: recall the reactions (reagents and conditions) by which alkanes can be produced: (a) addition of hydrogen to an alkene in a hydrogenation reaction, $\ce{H2(g)}$ and Pt/Ni catalyst and heat (b) cracking of a longer chain alkane, heat with $\ce{Al2O3}$

title: Combustion and substitution reactions of alkanes
statement: describe: (a) the complete and incomplete combustion of alkanes (b) the free-radical substitution of alkanes by $\ce{Cl2}$ or $\ce{Br2}$ in the presence of ultraviolet light, as exemplified by the reactions of ethane

title: Free-radical substitution mechanism
statement: describe the mechanism of free-radical substitution with reference to the initiation, propagation and termination steps

title: Cracking crude oil fractions
statement: suggest how cracking can be used to obtain more useful alkanes and alkenes of lower $M_r$ from heavier crude oil fractions

title: Unreactivity of alkanes
statement: understand the general unreactivity of alkanes, including towards polar reagents in terms of the strength of the $\ce{C-H}$ bonds and their relative lack of polarity

title: Environmental impact of alkane combustion
statement: recognise the environmental consequences of carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and unburnt hydrocarbons arising from the combustion of alkanes in the internal combustion engine and of their catalytic removal

title: Preparing alkenes: elimination and dehydration
statement: recall the reactions (including reagents and conditions) by which alkenes can be produced: (a) elimination of $\ce{HX}$ from a halogenoalkane by ethanolic $\ce{NaOH}$ and heat (b) dehydration of an alcohol, by using a heated catalyst (e.g. $\ce{Al2O3}$) or a concentrated acid (e.g. concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$) (c) cracking of a longer chain alkane

title: Electrophilic addition and oxidation of alkenes
statement: describe the following reactions of alkenes: (a) the electrophilic addition of (i) hydrogen in a hydrogenation reaction, $\ce{H2(g)}$ and Pt/Ni catalyst and heat (ii) steam, $\ce{H2O(g)}$ and $\ce{H3PO4}$ catalyst (iii) a hydrogen halide, $\ce{HX(g)}$, at room temperature (iv) a halogen, $\ce{X2}$ (b) the oxidation by cold dilute acidified $\ce{KMnO4}$ to form the diol (c) the oxidation by hot concentrated acidified $\ce{KMnO4}$ leading to the rupture of the carbon-carbon double bond and the identities of the subsequent products to determine the position of alkene linkages in larger molecules (d) addition polymerisation exemplified by the reactions of ethene and propene

title: Bromine water test for C=C bonds
statement: describe the use of aqueous bromine to show the presence of a $\ce{C=C}$ bond

title: Mechanism of electrophilic addition
statement: describe the mechanism of electrophilic addition in alkenes, using bromine/ethene and hydrogen bromide/propene as examples

title: Inductive effects and Markovnikov addition
statement: describe and explain the inductive effects of alkyl groups on the stability of primary, secondary and tertiary cations formed during electrophilic addition (this should be used to explain Markovnikov addition)
